definition.text: Interest is the extra money a borrower pays a lender, on top of paying back the amount borrowed, at a set rate.

facts.text: A bank customer usually pays interest to borrow, paying back more than was lent, and earns interest on savings, withdrawing more than was deposited.
Unlike a dividend, which a company shares out from profit, interest is paid at a rate fixed beforehand.
In economics the interest rate is the price of credit and acts as the cost of capital.
One explanation for interest rates usually being above zero is that loanable funds are scarce.
In the sixteenth century Martín de Azpilcueta argued that a good now is better than the same good later, so interest pays the lender for giving up spending in the meantime.
Sumerian documents from 3000 BC show systematic lending of grain and metals, and interest seems to have been well established by then.
Jacob Bernoulli is thought to have discovered the constant e by studying what happens as interest is compounded more and more often.

definition.text: Simple interest is interest worked out only on the original amount owed, without adding interest on earlier interest.

facts.text: It can be applied over periods other than a year, for example every month.
On a $2500 credit card balance at 12.99% a year applied monthly, one month's simple interest is $27.06.
Compound interest differs by also earning interest on interest already accumulated.

definition.text: The rule of 72 estimates how many years money takes to double: divide 72 by the yearly interest rate in percent.

facts.text: At 6 percent a year, money doubles in about 72/6 = 12 years.
The rule gives a good indication for interest rates up to 10%.

definition.text: Market interest rates are set in markets such as the money market, bond market and banks, and each loan's rate reflects several factors.

facts.text: Lenders weigh opportunity cost, the other uses of their money, including the return from competing investments.
A lender putting off consumption wants at least enough to cover price rises from inflation; nominal interest is roughly the real rate plus inflation.
A risk premium covers the chance of default, so loans to developing countries carry higher premiums than loans to the US government.
Shorter loans usually carry less default and inflation risk, so short-term rates are often below long-term rates, an upward sloping yield curve.
Investors want a higher return on an asset that is hard to resell quickly at a fair price than on a liquid one.
Central banks strongly influence short-term rates, one of the main tools of monetary policy.

definition.text: Theories of interest are the explanations different schools of economic thought have offered for why interest exists and what sets its rate.

facts.text: Aristotle and the Scholastics held that money is by nature sterile, so it was unjust to charge for being parted from it.
In the classical theory of Mill and others, the interest rate adjusts to balance the demand for borrowing with the supply of lending.
Wicksell's 1898 Interest and Prices distinguished natural from nominal interest rates; Ohlin and Robertson later refined this into the loanable funds theory.
In Keynes's 1936 General Theory, interest is set by the demand for money, liquidity preference, against a given money supply.

title: Internal rate of return

definition.text: The internal rate of return (IRR) is the yearly rate of return at which the net present value of all of an investment's cash flows equals zero.

facts.text: It is called internal because it ignores outside factors such as the risk-free rate, inflation, the cost of capital or financial risk.
Used before the fact it estimates a future annual return; used afterwards it measures the return actually achieved.
A project whose estimated IRR exceeds the firm's cost of capital for it is profitable.
IRR measures an investment's profitability or efficiency, while net present value measures how much value it adds.
For cash flows of -123,400, then 36,200, 54,800 and 48,100 over three years, the IRR is 5.96%.
In savings and loans the IRR is also called the effective interest rate.

title: Problems with the internal rate of return
article: Internal rate of return#Problems with use

definition.text: The internal rate of return has known flaws as a decision rule, chiefly that ranking projects by it can disagree with ranking them by net present value.

facts.text: When the aim is to maximise total value, IRR should not be used to choose between mutually exclusive projects: a bigger project can have a lower IRR but a higher NPV.
Despite a strong academic preference for NPV, surveys show executives prefer IRR.
When cash flows change sign more than once, a project may have several IRRs, and it is unclear whether high or low is better.
Whether IRR hides an assumption that all cash flows are reinvested is debated: some sources say yes, others say no.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether the IRR assumes cash flows are reinvested at the IRR until the project ends.

definition.text: Intertemporal choice is the study of how people value payoffs that arrive at different times, usually simplified to now versus some future date.

facts.text: John Rae introduced the idea in 1834; Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk in 1889 and Irving Fisher in 1930 developed the model further.
Consuming something today means it cannot be consumed in the future, so choices trade present against future consumption.
Diminishing marginal utility is a key idea used to analyse intertemporal choice, along with choice under uncertainty and social welfare.
Uncertain fuel prices and high discount rates for running costs make energy-efficiency investments look riskier to many decision makers.

definition.text: The Fisher model shows how a consumer with present and future income, able to lend or borrow at an interest rate, chooses between consuming now and later.

facts.text: It assumes constant income and utility maximisation, and treats investments as generators of savings.
With present income Y(t), future income Y(t+1) and interest rate r, the most one can consume now is Y(t) + Y(t+1)/(1+r).
The most one can consume in the future is (1+r)Y(t) + Y(t+1).
